title: Mouse, keyboard, serial lease, VMware pointer
summary:
The input subsystem is one of the kernel's strongest areas, and almost every rule in it traces to a named field machine. Each serial port decodes independently. The port contest weighs the identify burst, clean-packet runs, line errors and DSR/DCD, which is more evidence than any DOS-era driver used. Four backends end in one mou_apply and one mou_settle. The ISRs run on a private stack that sets SS as well as SP, waits are timed in ticks rather than spin counts, and the 32-bit VMware protocol is kept out of both shipped kernels. The weak spots are at the edges of the hardware model:
- A 16550 whose FIFO is already on is treated as an 8250 (input-1).
- The tick can park an AT ROM's int 09h with IRQ1 still in service, on the int 15h and kern_mega paths that SPEC 9.8.3 left unmasked. Under int 13h's sch_lock that becomes a predicted floppy timeout (input-2).
- After the contest settles, the serial ISR keeps reading retired and foreign UARTs and drops their bytes (input-3).
- SPEC 115 makes pinning the serial lease's ring the caller's duty, and nothing enforces it (input-4, R1).
Each fix is a handful of bytes and none needs an ABI break. The largest byte lever is the keyboard mouse: about 456 resident bytes on every machine, a textbook on-demand module that is still resident (R2). Comments and SPEC have drifted in about thirty places: names folded away (mou_claim), constants that moved (MOU_DRAINT 9 to 18), and a SPEC 9 intro that still describes the pre-9.5.2 ISR and the pre-kern_emu VMware arrangement.

strengths.title: Per-port decoders and an evidence-weighted contest
strengths.why: A modem's resync cannot break the mouse's run, and a losing device cannot move the arrow or click while it loses. The identify burst is read in the one window where the kernel owns the port outright, and line errors bar a port from the run. No DOS driver weighed this much evidence.

strengths.title: One back end, one settle
strengths.why: The binding both-buttons fall-through and the blk_act, cur_shchk and ui_post stores exist exactly once for serial, PS/2, driver and VMware. This is the pattern to copy wherever two producers feed one state machine.

strengths.title: Ticks rather than spin counts, and every elapsed time is wrap-safe
strengths.why: One constant means the same thing on a 4.77 MHz XT and on a 486.

strengths.title: The private ISR stack sets SS as well as SP, with no register
strengths.why: It survives a ROM service that switched stacks (SeaBIOS) and costs about 48 bytes off every task slice.

strengths.title: The overrun guard predicts nothing
strengths.why: It winds the tail back on a full buffer whatever byte arrives, which makes the nested-beep hang impossible rather than unlikely.

strengths.title: Vector hygiene
strengths.why: kbm_isr refuses to chain to itself, mouse_unhook restores int 09h or int 15h by [kbm_ivec], and the step byte records that int 74h is ours. Together these close the SPEC 9.6.5 freeze class.

strengths.title: KBD_I15: one vector, decided once
strengths.why: The scancode comes from the ROM's own read wherever an 8042 would lose a byte to a peek, and an XT pays nothing for it.

strengths.title: The probe is split by lifetime
strengths.why: The probe lives in .ovl/.boot2. Everything that hotplug or unhook can reach stays resident, each edge is named in tests/ovlrefs.txt, and the far doors share one stub.

strengths.title: The serial lease is nothing resident beyond routing
strengths.why: The module lives only while a lease is held. A leased row is routed through the existing ISR scan, so it inherits the cross-wired IRQ handling.

strengths.title: kern_emu isolates the 386 protocol
strengths.why: VMM_POLL assembles to zero bytes on both shipped kernels.

strengths.title: The published 'MO' block is asserted by offset
strengths.why: It is read on the one machine with no debugger and is treated as an ABI.

strengths.title: mouproto.inc is shared as source with kern_dos
strengths.why: It carries the arithmetic and nothing else, which is CLAUDE.md's shared-source rule applied correctly.

findings.title: A 16550 whose FIFO is already on is treated as an 8250
findings.detail: mouse_init programs LCR, DLL, DLM, MCR and IER and flushes RX, LSR and IIR, but never writes FCR (base+2). The ISR reads one RX byte per port per interrupt, and the SPEC 9.13 re-arm rewrites only MCR and IER. If an earlier OS, a warm-booted driver or a DOS program under DOS.O88 left the FIFO enabled, two things can happen. At trigger level 14 the pointer lags about 117 ms at 1200 baud and drains at one byte per four character times. At trigger level 1, two bytes queued during any IF=0 hold longer than 8.3 ms leave INTR asserted after the single read. The edge-triggered 8259 sees no new edge, and the mouse is silent for the session (SPEC 9.5.2's stuck-line symptom by another road).
evidence: kernel/mouse.inc:767-800 UART programming, no FCR write
kernel/mouse.inc:3720-3753 one RX read per port per IRQ
kernel/mouse.inc:1585-1590 the 9.13 re-arm writes MCR/IER only
SPEC.md:213126 nothing in the tree touches FCR
findings.recommendation: Write FCR=0 in mouse_init beside the LCR writes (mov ax,0x0200 / call mou_ov_pall); an 8250 ignores the write. Do the same in osapi_mouse's 9.13 re-arm. Optionally re-read the same row's LSR after mou_byte (pop bx / jmp short .scan), so no byte is ever left behind.
findings.bytes_est: +6 .ovl (kern_big) / +6 .boot2 (kern_small), 0 resident; +6 .text kern_big for the 9.13 re-arm; optional +2 .text both kernels
findings.prior_art: Every DOS comm driver and Windows' COMM.DRV either disables the FIFO or drains it in a loop until IIR reports no interrupt.
findings.verify_note: Re-read mouse.inc 767-900 and 1570-1590: no write to base+2 anywhere in kernel/ (grep FCR/fifo finds only a comment saying the 8250 has no FIFO). The scan takes one RX per row and moves on, so a FIFO holding a byte at or above trigger 1 keeps INTR high with no new edge. The in-session path (a DOS program enables the FIFO, exits, and the 9.13 re-arm rewrites MCR/IER only) is the likeliest trigger. Not measured. mov ax,imm16 + call near = 6 bytes, so the estimate holds.

findings.title: The tick can park a ROM int 09h with IRQ1 still in service, on the paths SPEC 9.8.3 left unmasked
findings.detail: On a KBD_I15 machine (kern_big on an AT ROM that advertises 4Fh), kbm_isr is not in the int 09h chain, so the ROM's handler is entered directly from IRQ1. kern_mega keeps a jmp far. sch_isr switches on every tick when sch_lock, chbusy and coop are clear and SS is LOW_SEG, without asking whether it interrupted an interrupt handler. The IBM AT int 09h executes sti at entry and sends its EOI only at the end. SPEC 9.8.3 exempts these paths because the AT ROM disables the keyboard interface; that covers a nested second byte but not a park. A tick inside the handler can switch to another task, for example the UI task that kbm_i15's sch_wake_ui has just made runnable. IRQ1 then stays in service until the parked task is next scheduled, and that blocks IRQ2-7. The serial mouse overruns and the PS/2 mouse on the cascade stalls. If the running task enters int 13h, which holds sch_lock for the whole call, the parked task cannot run at all: the floppy's IRQ6 cannot be delivered, the BIOS times out after about 2 s, and the call returns a disk error. PREDICTED, not measured. SeaBIOS does not sti in its IRQ handlers, so QEMU and Bochs cannot show it.
evidence: kernel/mouse.inc:3016-3019 the I15 path skips the IMR bracket
kernel/mouse.inc:3079-3099 kbm_i15 wakes the UI task
SPEC.md:16220-16258 9.8.3, IRQ1 'stays in service for as long as the handler is stretched or parked'
findings.recommendation: Adopt the generic rule: sch_isr refuses a switch while any IRQ other than IRQ0 is in service. Read the master ISR with OCW3 0Bh, test AL & 0FEh, and restore 0Ah; khb_* already uses this sequence at sched.inc:1947-1953. This covers the 4Fh path, kern_mega's jump and any driver ISR that sti's. Coordinate with the scheduler review, and verify on 86Box with an AMI or Phoenix AT BIOS.
findings.bytes_est: +~14-16 .text resident (sched.inc), all kernels; ~40 cycles on the switch path only, ESTIMATED
findings.prior_art: AmigaOS Exec defers dispatch until the outermost interrupt returns. OS/2 1.x dispatches only on the way back to task time. DOS TSRs read the 8259 ISR before popping up.
findings.verify_note: Re-read kbm_isr (2960-3060), kbm_i15 (3079-3100), sch_isr's switch gates (sched.inc 2380-2420) and SPEC 9.8.3. The I15 and kern_mega paths bypass the IMR bracket, and nothing in sch_isr reads the ISR before switching; sch_switch's only extra test is SS == LOW_SEG, which an AT ROM's int 09h (no stack hop) passes. Detail tightened: in pre-emptive mode IRQ1 stays in service until the parked task is next scheduled, not necessarily for a whole UI pass. The disk-timeout case is real because disk.inc holds sch_lock across int 13h, so the parked task cannot run during the call. Still a prediction.

findings.title: After the contest, the ISR still reads retired and foreign UARTs and drops their bytes
findings.detail: mou_isr_body scans every row with a nonzero base on every interrupt, for the rest of the session, because mou_lockon leaves the bases in place for mouse_unhook. mou_byte then drops any byte from a row that is not [mou_port], after the RX read has already consumed it. LSR data-ready does not depend on IER, so a retired port that someone else re-arms is still drained. Example: a DOS program under DOS.O88 (or any package) drives COM2 while the mouse is on COM1. Every mouse IRQ4 also scans row 2, after row 0's mou_byte -> cur_move. A COM2 byte that arrives during the arrow move is taken and thrown away before the program's own IRQ3 handler can see it. At 9600 baud a byte arrives about once per cur_move. The lease avoids this only for programs that use it.
evidence: kernel/mouse.inc:3720-3753 the scan walks all rows
kernel/mouse.inc:3793-3798 a non-winner byte goes to .jbout after the RX read
findings.recommendation: Once [mou_seen] is set, scan only [mou_port]'s row and [ser_row]; losers are IER 0 and cannot be why a line fired. For example, after the ser_row test: cmp byte [mou_seen],0 / je .take / cmp bl,[mou_port] / jne .next. Cross-wired machines are unaffected, because the mouse's own row is always scanned. Two-port machines also save one IN per row per IRQ.
findings.prior_art: Neither Windows 3.x's mouse driver nor OS/2 reads a UART it has not claimed; COMM.DRV and COM.SYS own their ports exclusively.
findings.verify_note: Re-read mou_isr_body .scan (3720-3753), mou_lockon (1215-1270) and mou_byte's head (3789-3798). Bases stay nonzero after lockon, the scan reads RX on any data-ready row, and mou_byte drops non-[mou_port] rows once [mou_seen] is set. The suggested sequence is 5+2+4+2 = 13 bytes, so the estimate moves from ~11 to ~13.

findings.title: The serial lease trusts its caller to pin the region the ISR writes into
findings.detail: srl_open validates the instance record, ES == I_SPTR and SI+517 <= I_SIZE, but never checks the region's MC_RLOC. It banks ES, and srl_pump then writes [es:si+...] from IRQ context. SPEC 115 makes the pin the caller's written duty ('The caller must pin its own region with OSAPI_MEM_MOVABLE, AX=0, before opening'), and the one caller, WireFleet, complies at wflink.inc:118-121. Every package must declare OS88_REGION_MOVABLE, though, so a caller that forgets the pin, or opts back in while leased, is moved by the next compaction. The ISR then keeps writing paragraphs that belong to another claim. That is silent corruption rather than 'lost bytes', and nothing enforces the contract.
evidence: kernel/serial.inc:226-243 the validation, with no MC_RLOC test
kernel/serial.inc:423-470 srl_pump writes from the ISR
SPEC.md:225404-225405 the pin is the caller's contract
findings.recommendation: (a) Have the module refuse Open with AX=5 when the region record's MC_RLOC != 0 (kern_big only; kern_small has no compaction), or (b) better, R1: move the ring into SERIAL.DRV's own image.
findings.listed_as: docs/reports/CODE-REVIEW-TWO-CYCLES-2026-11-01.md, Video bullet: 'A serial lease whose ring is inside the package's own region can lose bytes'
findings.prior_art: Windows 3.x OpenComm allocates its queues in the driver's own fixed memory.
findings.verify_note: The code is as stated: srl_open (serial.inc:207-275) has no MC_RLOC test, and srl_pump writes through the banked ES. The reviewer missed that SPEC 115 (225404-225405) states the pin as the caller's contract on purpose, and that the only caller complies. This is unenforced hardening of a documented contract, not a latent defect in shipped code, so severity drops from medium to low. The fix stays worthwhile.

findings.title: Shift+PrtSc runs the ROM's Print Screen inside kbm_isr's IRQ mask
findings.detail: On the kern_big int 09h path and on kern_small, kbm_isr calls the ROM with every IRQ but IRQ1 masked, and nothing hooks int 05h. On an 83-key keyboard PrtSc is Shift + keypad '*', so it is easy to press by accident. The ROM then walks 2,000 cells through int 10h AH=08h and int 17h with the clock, the scheduler, the serial mouse and the floppy masked. That is seconds with no printer, and tens of seconds while printing. Ticks are lost and the clock drifts. Separately, while an FSXF_RATE sample ISR plays, every keystroke now delays IRQ0 by up to about 1,725 cycles.
evidence: kernel/mouse.inc:3021-3031 the IMR bracket around the ROM call
no write to IVT 14h anywhere in kernel/ (grep)
SPEC.md:16162 the ROM's Print Screen path EOIs early
SPEC.md:37323 0x500 is the print-screen status byte
findings.recommendation: Set the BIOS print-screen status byte at linear 0500h to 1 in mouse_init; the IBM ROM's int 05h returns immediately while it reads 1, and DOS uses the same byte. Re-set it after a hibernate resume, which stages data over 0500h. Alternatively hook int 05h to an existing iret and restore it in mouse_unhook.
findings.bytes_est: +5 .ovl/.boot2, 0 resident (the int 05h hook alternative is about +12, partly resident)
findings.prior_art: Windows 3.x takes PrtSc for itself (a clipboard snapshot); DOS treats 0050:0000 as the in-progress flag.
findings.verify_note: grep finds no int 05h vector write in kernel/; the shipped arm's mask is 0FDh around the ROM call, so IRQ0 is masked for the whole Print Screen. hiber.inc:143 (KDS_LB at 0x0500) confirms the resume caveat. One side effect to note: setting 0500h=1 also disables Print Screen for DOS programs under DOS.O88.

findings.title: The 'MO' block publishes the doctored 8042 command byte as 'the BIOS's'
findings.detail: mou_p2cmd0 is the BIOS byte with bit 4 cleared and bit 5 forced set. The raw byte, mou_p2cmdr, is stored outside the published span. The code comment and SPEC 9.4.4 both say the span holds the byte 'as the machine's own BIOS left it'; the comment also says every failure path puts it back, but the failure paths restore mou_p2cmdr. Bit 5 is exactly SPEC 9.9.7's field defect (PC MODE on an AT controller), so a sysbench reading from that kind of machine cannot show how the BIOS left it. MOUDIAG's cmd column has the same problem.
findings.recommendation: Swap the two declarations so the raw byte sits at +6 inside the asserted span and the doctored one below it. Rename them so mou_p2_off keeps writing the doctored byte and .fail the raw one. Fix the declaration comment in the same change.
findings.verify_note: mouse.inc:1901-1912: cmdr = BIOS & 0EFh, cmd0 = that | 20h; only cmd0 is inside the published span (6466-6469). No doc fix is emitted here: rewriting SPEC 9.4.4 or the declaration comment to say 'doctored' would be undone by the recommended swap, so the comment belongs to the code change.

findings.title: srl_open's 'settled' test lags the ISR by one UI pass
findings.detail: srl_open treats the contest as settled only when [mou_hpst] == 2, and mou_hotplug's .have arm sets that on the pass after the ISR settled the contest. Inside that window, an Open the user named (BL bit 7), or one where the other port identified, takes the port the mouse has just won. The ISR then routes that row to SERIAL.DRV, and the mouse is dead until Close. That breaks SPEC 115.1's rule that 'a winning serial mouse's port is never eligible'.
evidence: kernel/serial.inc:323-334 the .unsettled rules 2 and 3 take the port
kernel/mouse.inc:3911-3916 the settle happens in the ISR
kernel/mouse.inc:1371-1379 hpst=2 is set only on the next pass
findings.recommendation: Test [mou_seen] instead (cmp byte [mou_seen],0 / je .unsettled); the settled arm already compares [mou_port].
findings.verify_note: serial.inc:265-268 tests [mou_hpst]; mou_hotplug sets 2 only in .have, on the next pass after [mou_seen]. In .unsettled, rules 2 and 3 can take the winning row, and mou_lockon later skips it because it equals [mou_port]. Swapping the compare is the same size (5+2 bytes).

findings.title: KBDDIAG=1 drops SPEC 9.8.3's IMR bracket, so the diagnostic build re-creates the defect it exists to diagnose
findings.detail: The KBD_DIAG arm calls the ROM with every IRQ open; the shipped arm masks all but IRQ1. kbddiag.inc's header still says the only change is call versus jump, which stopped being true when the shipped kernel began calling the ROM too. The field kernel built to diagnose keyboard faults therefore lets a tick run inside the ROM's handler again.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the diagnostic call in the same in 21h / push / or FDh / out ... pop / out bracket, then fix the header.
findings.verify_note: Both arms re-read: the KBD_DIAG arm is pushf / call far [cs:kbm_old9] with no IMR write. The header doc fix emitted here describes the current code (no bracket); if the code fix lands, its last clause goes with it.

findings.title: mou_p2_off writes the 8042 on the UI task with nothing excluding int 09h
findings.detail: mou_p2_off sends 0A7h and then the command-byte pair (60h, then the value) with IF=1 and IRQ1 live. An AT ROM's int 09h writes 0ADh and 0AEh to port 64h. If IRQ1 lands between the two halves, the pending controller command is replaced, the value byte goes to port 60h with nothing pending, and the 8042 forwards it to the keyboard; the command byte is never restored. mou_p2_init masks IRQ1 for exactly this class of race. The path runs only when a serial mouse beats a live PS/2 mouse, and at unhook.
findings.recommendation: Bank and mask IRQ1 at the master around the two writes, as the probe does. Do not use pushf/cli: mou_p2wr's timeout counts ticks.
findings.verify_note: mou_p2_off masks only IRQ12 at the slave; mou_p2wcmd writes 60h to 64h, then the value to 60h after mou_p2wr's tick-timed wait. The probe's IRQ1 mask comment (1848-1863) describes the same race.

findings.title: PS/2 sync rests on byte 0's bit 3 alone
findings.detail: The decoder re-syncs only by refusing a header without bit 3. The probe flushes the 8042 buffer after F4 has enabled reporting, which can cut a packet in half. A misaligned stream then takes b1 or b2 as a header whenever bit 3 happens to be set. Until it realigns, the low bits read as buttons (phantom clicks) and the deltas are garbage. A hot-replugged device's AA 00 is taken as a header.
findings.recommendation: Reset [mou_p2ph] to 0 when [ticks] has moved by 2 or more since the last aux byte. A packet's bytes arrive within milliseconds and packets are at least 10 ms apart.
findings.prior_art: Linux psmouse's lost-sync timeout; Windows i8042prt's per-packet timer.
findings.verify_note: mou_p2_byte's only sync is test al,08h on phase 0; mou_p2flush follows F4 before 0AEh. 0AAh has bit 3 set. This is a plausible weakness, not an observed one.

findings.title: The hot-plug poller drops DTR on a modem port every 3 s for the whole session
findings.detail: While [mou_seen] is 0, mou_hotplug power-cycles every unleased live port through mou_pall. It stops only on an identify or a PS/2 answer. On a mouseless XT with a modem each drop is a hang-up (&D2), and an os8088 null-modem peer sees DSR/DCD flicker. SPEC 115.1.1's rule 4 already treats DSR/DCD as 'not a mouse'.
findings.recommendation: Skip the drop on a port whose MSR shows DSR or DCD (the lease's own rule), which makes the drop per port inside mou_hotplug only.
findings.prior_art: MOUSE.COM and Windows 3.x probed once at load and never power-cycled a port they could not identify.
findings.verify_note: MOU_REPOLL = 55 ticks (~3 s); mou_pall/mou_pout skip only [ser_row] and zero bases, so a modem port loses DTR each cycle. It also rewrites MCR under any DOS program driving that port.

findings.title: The keyboard mouse is about 456 resident bytes on every machine and qualifies as an on-demand module
findings.detail: Measured from build/kernel.map: kbm_tab..kbm_isr less mou_clamp is 306 bytes, kbm_p5spend 16, kbm_pollm..kbm_ui 108, kbm_post 9, plus 17 bytes of state. This is resident on both kernels, and on most machines a mouse retires it seconds after boot (SPEC 9.6.1.1). It is needed only when someone presses an arrow on a pointerless desktop, and loading it then needs the system disk in the drive. Its own header calls it 'a FIRST CANDIDATE TO REMOVE'; a module is the middle road. See R2.
evidence: build/smallk/kernel.map 0x3054-0x31A6 (306 less mou_clamp, the same span)
findings.recommendation: Keep resident only kbm_key's two gates, KBM_SCAN's keypad-5 latch, kbm_shf, and thunks for the claim path, kbm_poll/kbm_pollm, kbm_ui and kbm_p5spend. Move the table, button, rclick, move, the kbm_ui body and the state into a KBMOUSE module loaded on the first claimed key, and drop it when [mou_ptr] is set (t_moddrop requires the drop).
findings.bytes_est: -300 to -380 resident on both kernels, +~450 module, ESTIMATED; the first press costs one disk read (~400 ms on an XT)
findings.verify_note: Spans re-measured from build/kernel.map and they match: 306 + 16 + 108 + 9 + 17 = 456. kern_small's kbm_tab..kbm_isr span is the same 306 once mou_clamp is taken out. Whether it qualifies under CLAUDE.md's module rule depends on accepting a system-disk read at the moment the mouse has failed; that is a judgement for the owner, not a defect.

findings.title: Keys are dispatched before clicks queued in the same pass
findings.detail: ui_task polls int 16h first and sends the key to wm_top, and only then drains the event ring that holds the clicks. If a click on a window and the typing after it land in one pass, the keys go to the window that was in front before the click. On an XT a pass that repaints lasts hundreds of milliseconds, so the window for this is real. See R3.
evidence: kernel/ui.inc:134-136 the key poll comes first
findings.recommendation: Measure how often it happens first. A partial fix: kbm_isr already calls the ROM on most paths, so it can compare the BIOS tail before and after and push an ordering marker into the ring; ui_task takes a key from int 16h only when it pops a marker. The 4Fh path and kern_mega keep today's behaviour.
findings.bytes_est: +~30 resident plus one appended EVT_* code (an ABI addition, not a break), ESTIMATED
findings.prior_art: Windows 3.x's system queue, the Mac Event Manager, the GEOS Input Manager and AmigaOS input.device all keep keyboard and mouse in one time-ordered stream.
findings.verify_note: ui.inc 134-256 re-read: int 16h AH=01h and the wm_top dispatch run before .events drains the ring. The byte estimate is unverified.

findings.title: A settled serial mouse is never offered a reset edge again
findings.detail: [mou_hpst]=2 is terminal. SPEC 9.4 opens with the wedge: a mouse hot-plugged onto live DTR stays wedged until it is power-cycled. After a settle that stays true for the rest of the session, for example after the cable is bumped.
findings.recommendation: Record it. If it is ever wanted, add a Control Panel verb or a key combination that runs one drop-hold-raise on [mou_port] alone; the machinery already exists.
findings.verify_note: mou_hotplug's first compare returns on state 2 for the rest of the session.

findings.title: mou_b0 and mou_b1 live in the high bytes of other tables' words, guarded only by prose
findings.detail: mou_b0 is mou_phase+1 and mou_b1 is mou_masks+1. The only guard is the comment 'READ AS BYTES ONLY'. A future word read of mou_masks would silently return a packet byte, which is the kind of invariant CLAUDE.md wants held by a gate rather than by a comment.
findings.recommendation: Keep the 4 bytes and add a tests/unit grep that refuses word reads of mou_masks and mou_phase, or spend the 4 bytes.
findings.verify_note: mouse.inc:6291 and 6298 define the two equs. Note that mou_newround already does word writes to mou_phase, which are intended and clear b0 too.

findings.title: mou_claim no longer exists, and 22 references remain
findings.detail: mou_claim was folded into mou_byte's .pkt arm in kernel size pass 17. Ten kernel comments and twelve SPEC lines still name it, most of them as live code.
findings.recommendation: Write 'mou_byte's .pkt arm (mou_claim until size pass 17)' once in SPEC 9.5.1.1, and name MOU_SETTLE_STORES or mou_settle where a line means the stores. A checkdocs rule for retired labels in backticks would stop the next one.
findings.verify_note: grep confirms. The doc fixes below cover every present-tense reference. The past-tense or cost-record ones are left as history: mouse.inc 1385 and 1491, and SPEC 14865, 14903, 15335 and 17602. vmmouse.inc:333 was an extra hit the reviewer missed.

findings.title: The two diagnostic knobs carry two copies of one formatter
findings.detail: The mdg_tpl/line/h16/h8/h1 and kbg_tpl/line/h* routines are the same code. The knobs are mutually exclusive, so no shipped byte is spent and the cost is maintenance only. The mdg_* copy learned to use hand loops because ES is not its own, while kbg_show sets ES itself.
findings.recommendation: Factor the formatter into a diagfmt.inc the next time either knob is touched.
findings.verify_note: Both files define the parallel tpl/line/h16/h8/h1 set (moudiag 440-537, kbddiag 518-592), and kbddiag.inc:31-33 refuses both knobs at once.

findings.title: The serial ISR saves all nine registers for every byte
findings.detail: The full frame costs about 650 cycles per byte (about 136 µs), roughly 1.6% of an XT while the hand moves at 1200 baud, ESTIMATED from PERFORMANCE Part 2's tables. Phase-1 and phase-2 bytes need only AX, BX, DX and DS. A light path would save about 0.25% of the machine.
findings.recommendation: Not worth its bytes. Record the number so nobody re-derives it.
findings.verify_note: Low-severity perf record, not re-derived. The frame is nine push/pop pairs as stated, but the cycle figure was not checked against PERFORMANCE.md.

doc_fixes.old_text: ; mouse_x/mouse_y themselves range over the full 0..639 / 0..479.
doc_fixes.new_text:
; mouse_x/mouse_y themselves range over the live screen, 0..[vid_wm1] /
; 0..[vid_hm1] - or both displays' union on a two-display kern_big
; (mou_clamp, SPEC.md 39.15.4).

doc_fixes.old_text:
- ISR: `mou_isr` (IRQ4) and `mou_isr3` (IRQ3) differ only in the port row
  each hands the shared body in BX — the one register that can be spent
  before DS is loaded and still index a table afterwards, so it is pushed
  *first* and popped *last*, and it stays the port row all the way to the
  completed packet because **every port decodes independently** (§9.5). Then:
  save the remaining registers + DS/ES, load DS=KERNEL_SEG, read that port's
  RX register — **always**, whatever is to be done with the byte, because the
  read is what clears the UART's interrupt — assemble packet
doc_fixes.new_text:
- ISR: `mou_isr` (IRQ4) and `mou_isr3` (IRQ3) differ only in the 8259 bit
  each stamps into `[mou_lfired]` (§9.5.2.1). The shared body switches to
  its own stack (§9.10), saves the registers + DS/ES, loads DS=KERNEL_SEG
  and scans **every live port**, not the one the vector is named for
  (§9.5.2): an LSR read each, and that port's RX read wherever a byte is
  waiting — the read is what clears that UART's interrupt — handed to
  `mou_byte` with the port row in BX, which stays the row all the way to the
  completed packet because **every port decodes independently** (§9.5). A
  leased row goes to `SERIAL.DRV` instead (§115.2). Then: assemble packet
doc_fixes.why: mou_isr/mou_isr3 only stamp MOU_L4/MOU_L3 into [mou_lfired] (mouse.inc:3667-3686); mou_isr_body's .scan reads every live row's LSR and RX only on data-ready (3720-3753).
